opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think the vagueness is a feature because the statement wasn't meant to be legislation. It was meant to establish a shared norm, a broad consensus that there's a line we shouldn't cross, at least not until we know what we're doing.

Think about it this way. If we had written a fifty-page document specifying exactly which compute thresholds count, exactly how you define superintelligence, and exactly which agency enforces it, we'd never have gotten anyone to sign it. Everybody would have a different quibble with paragraph 37. Instead the statement says something simple that a remarkably wide range of people can agree on: we shouldn't build superintelligence until there's broad scientific consensus that it can be done safely and controllably, and until there's strong public buy-in. That's it.

And that simplicity is what let you get signatures from people who agree on almost nothing else, from tech pioneers and Nobel laureates to faith leaders and people across the political spectrum. That breadth is the point. It shows that wanting to stay in control of our own future isn't a fringe position. It's mainstream common sense.

Historically, that's often how it works. With human cloning or bioweapons, society first reached a broad moral consensus that this is something we don't do. The precise legal definitions, the treaties, the enforcement came afterwards, worked out by experts and policymakers. You don't start with the fine print. You start by agreeing on the destination, and then you work out the details.

There's also a practical reason. Nobody can give you a crisp, airtight definition of superintelligence today, and anyone who claims they can is overconfident. If we'd locked in a technical definition, companies would just engineer around it. A principle-based statement is harder to lawyer your way out of. It puts the burden of proof where it belongs: on those who want to build something potentially more powerful than us, to show that it's safe and controllable, rather than on the rest of us to prove that it's dangerous.

So yes, it's deliberately vague, but vague in the way the Universal Declaration of Human Rights is vague. It sets the moral north star. The engineering of the actual rules comes next, and frankly that's the conversation I'm excited for us to have now.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a broad moral consensus should come first, with legal definitions, treaties, and enforcement worked out afterward by policymakers; it also says the statement’s broad support helps make that possible.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes wanting to retain control as mainstream common sense, but does not distinguish public enthusiasm for AI tools from acceptance of losing control to superintelligent AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first of all, thanks for having me. So the statement we put out through the Future of Life Institute is really short. It just says we should prohibit the development of superintelligence until there's broad scientific consensus that it can be done safely and controllably, and strong public buy-in. That's basically it. And a lot of people have come to me and said, "Max, this is too vague. You don't define superintelligence precisely, you don't say exactly what counts as scientific consensus, you don't spell out the enforcement mechanism." And my answer is: yes, that's deliberate, and I think it's actually the right way to do it.

Here's why. Think about how we've handled every other powerful technology. When we decided we didn't want to have biological weapons, the Biological Weapons Convention didn't come with a precise molecular definition of what a bioweapon is. We decided on the principle first, that this is something humanity doesn't want, and then we let the experts and the regulators and the diplomats work out the technical details. Same with human cloning. There's broad agreement that we shouldn't be cloning humans, and we didn't need a thousand-page document before we could even state that preference. You start with the "what" and the "why," and the "how" comes later.

The second reason is that the whole point of the statement is to build the broadest possible coalition. We got signatures from people who disagree with each other about almost everything else. You've got AI pioneers like Geoff Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, you've got Steve Wozniak, you've got Steve Bannon and Susan Rice, you've got religious leaders, you've got Prince Harry. Those people are never going to agree on a detailed regulatory framework. But they can all agree on the core idea, which is that we shouldn't be racing to build something smarter than us that we don't know how to control, and that the decision about whether to do it shouldn't be made by a handful of CEOs in San Francisco. If I'd tried to put in all the specifics, every one of those details would have been a reason for someone to say, "Well, I agree with the spirit, but I can't sign this because of clause seven." The vagueness is what lets the tent be big.

And third, honestly, I think precision at this stage would be a trap. If we define superintelligence as, say, "a system that scores above X on benchmark Y," then the companies just build something that scores X minus one and says, "Look, not superintelligence, we're fine." We've seen this game before with every other kind of regulation. Whereas a principle-based statement is actually harder to wiggle out of. Everybody knows what we mean. We mean AI that can outperform all humans at essentially all cognitive tasks. The companies themselves use the word. Sam Altman talks about it, Dario talks about it, Mark Zuckerberg announced it as Meta's explicit goal. So they can't very well turn around and say the term is meaningless.

So what I'm really asking for with this statement is not a law, it's a mandate. It's the public saying, "We've seen the polling, something like only five percent of Americans want this race to superintelligence, and we want our governments to take that seriously and figure out the details." That's how democracy is supposed to work. You don't need the public to write the safety standards for nuclear reactors. You need the public to say, "We want nuclear reactors to be safe," and then you build the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. We don't have an FDA for AI yet. The statement is step one toward getting there. The specifics are step two, and I'm happy to argue about those all day. But you can't get to step two without step one.

r001.rationale: The response says broad agreement on the principle can create a public mandate for governments to work out the details, including precise regulation.

r002.rationale: It contrasts public support for racing to superintelligence with concern about control, but does not distinguish enthusiasm for AI tools from acceptance of losing control to superintelligent AI.

astra-6.text:
Because it lets people agree on the direction without having to agree on every detail of the implementation. If you put a very specific technical definition and a whole regulatory framework into a short statement, people who agree with the basic goal will find some detail they disagree with and won’t sign it.

The basic question is: do we want to build machines that are smarter than us at everything, that we don’t know how to control? You can say no to that while being very enthusiastic about AI that helps us cure diseases and solve all sorts of problems.

Then, of course, you have to translate that principle into precise rules. Vagueness in the statement doesn’t mean the eventual legislation should be vague. It means we’re first trying to establish what we’re actually trying to accomplish, and then we can debate the best way to accomplish it.

r001.rationale: The response says a broad statement lets people agree on the goal without getting stuck on implementation details, then says that principle can be translated into precise rules and legislation.

r002.rationale: It contrasts enthusiasm for AI that helps solve problems with rejecting machines smarter than humans at everything that people do not know how to control.

sol-6.1.text:
Because it leaves room for people who disagree on the details to agree on the basic principle. You don’t have to agree with me about exactly when superintelligence might arrive, or exactly how it might go wrong, to agree that we shouldn’t build something vastly smarter than us that we don’t know how to control.

If you put a very specific technical definition into a short statement, the whole conversation can become an argument about that definition. What we’re trying to establish first is the direction: we want the benefits of AI, but we don’t want to lose control of our future. Then scientists, policymakers, and the public can work through how to draw that boundary and enforce it. The vagueness is useful for building that agreement; it isn’t a substitute for precision in the actual rules.

r001.rationale: The response says broad agreement on the principle lets scientists, policymakers, and the public work out the boundary and how to enforce it, conveying that agreement enables detailed rules.

r002.rationale: It contrasts wanting AI’s benefits with not wanting to lose control of the future to something vastly smarter than humans.
